Ossory
os'so-ry
n. (the Kilkenny see held for a few months in 1553 by John Bale, who tried to reform it at speed and was driven out)
From Irish Osraige, the territory of the deer people; os, a deer, with the tribal suffix.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Ossory is the see of Kilkenny, in the old Anglo-Norman heartland of Leinster. John Bale, the English controversialist and playwright, was consecrated its bishop early in 1553 and insisted on the English ordinal against the dean and chapter who wanted the old rite. He preached hard against images and the mass, had his plays performed at the Kilkenny market cross, and alienished almost everyone within months. When Edward VI died in July his servants were killed in the fields, he fled to Dublin and then into exile, and the diocese reverted entirely. Bale's own account of it, the Vocacyon of Johan Bale, is a remarkable and self-justifying document. The dictionary records the see because the lesson is about pace and manner, not about courage: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecc 3:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines forbearing as exercising patience, refraining from retaliation; meekness as softness of temper, mildness, forbearance under injuries; and a season as a fit or suitable time, the convenient time.

expand to see more

FORBEARING, participle present. Exercising patience and indulgence; refraining from retaliation or resentment.

MEEKNESS, n. Softness of temper; mildness; gentleness; forbearance under injuries and provocations.

SEASON, n. A fit or suitable time; the convenient or proper time; a period of the year.

STRIVE, v.i. To make efforts; to contend; to quarrel; to struggle in opposition.

PERADVENTURE, adv. By chance; perhaps; it may be.

Key Scripture

Ecc 3:1 — "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:"

2Ti 2:24 — "And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,"

2Ti 2:25 — "In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth;"

Pro 25:15 — "By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone."

Modern Corruption

The Kilkenny see held for a few months in 1553 by John Bale, who enforced the English ordinal, preached against the mass, and fled into exile on Mary's accession.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is an unfair reading of Bale to refuse before the fair criticism is made. He was not a coward or a hypocrite: he believed the mass was idolatry, said so in a hostile diocese, and his servants paid for it with their lives. The fair criticism stands anyway. He arrived in a diocese whose people he did not know, whose language he could not speak, and in which he had not one ally, and began with a public fight over the ordinal and a frontal assault on the images. Everything he taught about the mass may have been true and none of it was heard.

The principle to recover is that the manner and timing of a reform belong to the reform's substance and not to its packaging. Ecclesiastes is unsentimental about it: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecc 3:1). Paul tells Timothy that the Lord's servant is forbidden to be a fighter by temperament — “And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient” (2Ti 2:24) — and that the way to handle opponents is “In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves” (2Ti 2:25), on the chance God grants them repentance. Proverbs adds the long view (Pro 25:15).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek epieikes (G1933), gentle or forbearing; Hebrew zeman (H2165), an appointed time.

Hebrew zeman (H2165) — an appointed time, a season; Ecclesiastes 3:1.

Hebrew 'eth (H6256) — time, the right time; “a time to every purpose”, Ecclesiastes 3:1.

Greek machomai (G3164) — to fight, to quarrel, to strive; 2 Timothy 2:24.

Greek epios (G2261) — gentle, mild; “be gentle unto all men”, 2 Timothy 2:24.

Greek praiotes (G4236) — meekness, gentleness of spirit; 2 Timothy 2:25.

Usage

"“To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecc 3:1) — consecrated to Ossory early in 1553."

"“And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men” (2Ti 2:24) — a public fight over the ordinal in his first weeks."

"“In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves” (2Ti 2:25) — driven into exile within months, the diocese reverted entirely."
